To estimate the probabilities for when mathematical conjectures will be proven (e.g., P vs NP, Riemann hypothesis) in particular when several of the major conjectures will be proven, one might consider the following factors:

*   Rate at which breakthroughs occur:  If one considers the major breakthroughs in the last 5-10 years, there have been many that most people would totally be able to list.  If one more closely considers the past 20 years, there have been fewer and would take more time to list.
*   Scale of impact:  Generally speaking many people care about the applications while only a small portion of experts care about the proofs themselves.  That correlation implies that there are many useful猜想应用在日常中，但只有少数专家关心证明过程。换种说法，即使人们对理论问题不感兴趣，仍然可能有一些有趣的结果。For example, if you wanted to look at encryption, you could say that many people care about encryption, because it affects them in their day-to-day lives.  But very few people care about the details of encryption itself.  Whereas if you're into encryption, you'd read about the algorithm, and you'd try to learn as much as possible about how the cryptography actually works- and the cryptographic functions might have quite interesting properties that few people know of.  So there's this wide range of applications of cryptography, but there's also this narrow range of people who really understand how the cryptography itself functions.  In other words, there are many ways to apply cryptography and many reasons to do so without necessarily caring too much about its foundations.  This is also true for some of the most famous theoretical questions, including the P vs NP hypothesis.  Many people use computers without knowing what "P" and "NP" actually mean.  They can also use cryptography, even if they don't know how the cryptographic algorithms work.  Similarly, many people vote without knowing whether it is possible to design a voting system that is both fair and efficient, or whether a more powerful voting system is possible.  These are other examples of problems in computer science which most people don't Know how to solve, but which some people with expertise try to solve in order to improve public policy or create more efficient voting systems.

Notably, there is no consensus or hypothesis that P vs NP will ever be proven uncomputable.  Also, it seems there's no consensus or hypothesis that it will ever be proven undecidable.
